- **Hooks vs. classifiers**: This plan illustrates a common trap — a "readiness" classifier and the actual blocking gate must agree byte-for-byte, or the classifier becomes a false advertiser. Here, the pre-commit hook checks marker mtime > `STATE.md`, but the plan defers freshness to "warning only", so Lane B can advertise issues that will fail at commit time.

When a regex parser drives a Lane B gate, format drift becomes a silent correctness hazard.
- **Dogfooding paradox**: This is a plan about how to evaluate plans, and its own review artifacts are 0-byte stubs (Codex CLI 0.124.0 stdin-hang). The acceptance criterion that requires fanout-clean reviews can't be satisfied under the current regression — that mismatch needs to be resolved in the plan, not at execution time.

## Findings

1. **Plan header advertises review artifacts that don't carry content.** Line 7 lists `scripts/review/results/2026-04-26-plan-2489-{claude,codex,gemini}.md` as the plan's "Review artifacts". On disk these are 0-byte stubs (Claude, Codex) plus a 429-byte Gemini file — and during this review they vanished entirely, leaving only `.fuse_hidden*` markers. Plan body line 226 then says "Formal multi-provider plan review has not yet run." The header and body contradict each other, and a reader following the header link gets nothing.

2. **Acceptance criterion #221 cannot be satisfied today and the plan doesn't say how to handle it.** Line 221 requires `scripts/review/plan-review-fanout.sh` to produce reviews with all MAJOR findings resolved before moving to `status:plan-review`. Per the documented `feedback_codex_cli_0_124_upstream_regression` (issue #2479), Codex CLI 0.124.0 hangs on stdin and produces empty artifacts — exactly what we observe in the 0-byte `…codex.md`. The plan must either pin the workaround (downgrade to 0.123.0, or accept Codex `UNAVAILABLE` as non-blocking) or it cannot be advanced under its own rules.

3. **Lane B definition diverges from the pre-commit gate it's supposed to align with.** Acceptance criterion line 210 requires Lane B to have a "local issue-specific approval marker", and Risks line 246 explicitly defers freshness ("can be a warning unless review requires it as a hard gate"). But `scripts/enforcement/require-plan-approval.sh` line 52 enforces `-newer .planning/STATE.md`. Result: Lane B will publish issues as execution-ready that the actual hook will reject when an agent tries to commit. For a continuous-pipeline report whose entire job is overnight dispatch, this is a load-bearing inconsistency that must be locked, not deferred to "Open."

4. **Review-artifact pseudocode regex misses three of the four real filename generations.** Pseudocode line 135 says `scan scripts/review/results/*-plan-NNN-*.md`. Real artifacts include: `2026-04-23-plan-2438-r2-review-1.md`, `2026-04-23-plan-2438-r3-final-review.md`, `2026-04-23-plan-XXXX-disagreement.md`, and 93 legacy `20260209T204919Z-foamy-sprouting-scroll.md-plan-claude.md` style files (output of `ls scripts/review/results/ | grep -v standard pattern | head`). The MAJOR verdict recorded in an `-r3-final-review.md` will not be discovered, so an issue with an active MAJOR blocker can be falsely promoted to Lane B. No test in the list (lines 188-202) covers `-rN-` or `-r3-final-review` parsing.

5. **`status:plan-approved` issues with NO review artifact at all are undefined.** Acceptance criterion line 210 says Lane B requires "no MAJOR/FAIL/UNAVAILABLE review blocker". With 48 currently-approved open issues — most predating the 2026-04-23 fanout era — the missing-review case is the dominant case and the criterion is silent on it. Treat-as-blocker leaves Lane B near-empty; treat-as-pass voids the safety check. Pick one and write the test.

6. **No test exercises "approved + plan + marker + MAJOR review → not Lane B".** The TDD list (lines 188-202) tests MAJOR for Lane A approval candidates (`test_plan_with_major_review_is_not_approval_candidate`) and tests Lane B success (`test_classifies_lane_b_only_when_label_plan_review_and_marker_exist`), but doesn't cover the most dangerous case — a fully-evidenced approved issue whose latest review went MAJOR. Given finding #4, this is the path most likely to leak.

7. **Scope-isolation criterion (line 218) overlaps materially with #2129.** The plan's warning surface (`approved_no_marker`, `approved_no_plan`, `dual_status_labels`, `marker-without-open-approved-issue`) is drift detection by another name. Asserting "explicitly does not duplicate #2129" in prose while shipping operationally-overlapping warnings will create two truths-of-record. Either narrow the warnings to what feeds Lane decisions only, or rephrase the criterion to "consumes #2129 outputs when present" and define the consumption interface.

8. **Title and Deliverable claim "pipeline" but only the classifier+report are in scope.** Line 1 ("Continuous Planning Pipeline"), Deliverable (line 116-118), and #2489's stated "day/night loop" all imply dispatch. The Files-to-Change table delivers a report only, with `provider-work-queue.py` integration marked "Optional". No integration test covers report→dispatch handoff. Either retitle to "lane-readiness report" / split out a dispatch phase, or add a Files-to-Change row that wires the report into `provider-work-queue.py` / `generate_issue_prompts.py` and tests the handoff.

- **F1, F2, F3, F4** are blockers for moving #2489 to `status:plan-review`:

## Findings

1. **Approval-gate artifact metadata contract has no tooling backing.** Plan Status header (line 8) and Acceptance Criterion (line 295) require the gate runner to "copy latest non-empty fanout/fallback stdout into timestamped immutable artifacts, prepend `Reviewed-Commit:` and `Plan-SHA256:` metadata." The "Files to Change" table on lines 226–241 does not include `scripts/review/plan-review-fanout.sh`, nor any new gate-runner script, nor `scripts/review/lib/disagreement-diff.sh`. The plan therefore mandates an artifact contract it provides no implementation surface for. (Codex review §Findings #1, verified live.)

2. **Markdown section-order is simultaneously claimed policy-driven and hard-coded.** Plan Pseudocode (line 196) says "use existing v2 policy/ranking from `config/skills/weekly-audit-policy.yaml` … instead of hard-coding a second policy surface," and the canonical render path goes through `_write_markdown_artifact()`. But the very next paragraph (line 200) and Acceptance Criterion (line 284) hard-code an 11-section literal sequence: `New → Changed → Filesystem-only → Content Quality → Grouping → Oversized → Usage → Follow-up → Unresolved → Suppressed → Errors`. `config/skills/weekly-audit-policy.yaml:172–178` defines `ranking_policy.section_order` with only 5 abstract IDs (`new_findings`, `changed_findings`, `unresolved_high_confidence_findings`, `suppressed_carry_forward_findings`, `operational_errors_or_skipped_inputs`). The legacy family sections (`Content Quality`, `Grouping`, `Oversized`, `Usage`, `Follow-up`) appear nowhere in `weekly_summary_sections` (lines 160–170) or `ranking_policy.section_order`. The plan only adds `id: filesystem_only_inventory` to `weekly_summary_sections` — it does not propose extending `ranking_policy.section_order` to include the legacy family sections it now wants policy-bound. So either YAML is the source of truth (and the test on line 268 must fail) or the hard-coded sequence wins (and the policy-driven claim is false). Pick one. (Codex review §Findings #4, verified.)

3. **Sparse-checkout / partial-inventory acceptance gate is unimplementable from the pseudocode.** Acceptance Criterion (line 299) requires the audit to "report sparse checkout with the skills dir outside the sparse patterns, or returns a tracked count far below the tracked planning snapshot without an explicit override," and TDD test `test_sparse_checkout_or_partial_git_inventory_is_warned_not_trusted` (line 269) asserts "successful-but-partial git inventory does not create false loss findings." But Pseudocode (lines 160–166) only documents the failure path: "if test seam … else call git_list_fn or default git ls-files … never hard-code .claude/skills." There is no specified detection mechanism for a *successful* `git ls-files` returning a sparse view: no sparse-config probe (`git config core.sparseCheckout`), no `git sparse-checkout list` invocation, no threshold for "far below the planning snapshot," and no override flag named. A test cannot be written for behavior the design does not specify. (Codex review §Findings #3, verified — pseudocode has no sparse-detection helper.)

4. **Live inventory baseline drift in the Resource Intelligence Summary and Risks section.** Plan line 21 and line 324 cite `tracked 3028 / tracked_active 922 / filesystem 3100 / filesystem_active 928`. Re-running the plan's own embedded proof script on 2026-04-26 from the working tree yields `tracked 3030 / tracked_active 924 / filesystem 3102 / filesystem_active 930` — `+2` across all four counts. The 6 untracked active `SKILL.md` paths are unchanged. The plan acknowledges this drift class in Risks (line 324) and says implementation recomputes live, so this is not blocking, but the cited "verified 2026-04-25" snapshot is already stale at planning-time `+1 day` and either deserves a refresh or an explicit "snapshot-only, not gate evidence" annotation matching the same treatment given to mutable review artifacts.

5. **Codex review (the cited evidence) issued MAJOR; the plan's Adversarial Review Summary table understates its weight.** `scripts/review/results/2026-04-25-plan-2488-codex.md` returns `## Verdict\nMAJOR` with 4 numbered blockers. The plan's §Adversarial Review Summary row for Codex (line 309) describes the verdict as "scope creep, recurring-schema contradiction, vanished-path closeout ambiguity, and scheduled-task doc drift" — paraphrasing rather than naming the four concrete blockers (gate-artifact contract not implementable, schema-shape misstatement, sparse-checkout under-spec, section-order self-contradiction). Three of those four are still live in the current revision (Findings 1, 2, 3 above). The plan's own gate text (Acceptance Criterion 295) says "no unresolved MAJOR findings from available reviewers before the gate" — by its own rule, the plan cannot move to `status:plan-review` until those Codex blockers are demonstrably resolved.

6. **Acceptance Criterion 295 self-references a contract whose script is not yet built.** The criterion says provider artifacts must "record the reviewed plan commit or plan SHA256." No script in `scripts/review/` currently emits either. The plan has no Files-to-Change row creating such a wrapper. Same root cause as Finding 1, restated as an acceptance-criteria executability defect: an AC that no commit can satisfy is structurally MAJOR.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`

These are scope-shape defects, not codebase-misunderstanding defects — fixable by either (a) adding `scripts/review/plan-review-fanout.sh` and a small `gate-runner` to Files to Change with concrete metadata-emission specs, or (b) loosening AC 295 to match what the existing fanout actually produces.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The `stash@{N}^3` recovery pattern from memory worked exactly as advertised.** Per `feedback_stash_caret_3_for_untracked.md`: when Hermes stashed my untracked files, they landed in the third parent (`^3`) of each stash commit (the "untracked tree" tree-object), invisible to plain `git stash show`. Without that memory entry I would have tried `git stash apply` or `git stash show -p` and gotten empty results, then re-written from scratch. The memory saved ~10 minutes and prevented content drift between the original write and any re-creation.
- **Hermes' stash naming was the key forensic clue.** The temp-leftover stashes were time-ordered, and `git show stash@{N}^3 --stat` revealed which timestamp captured which file. Latest ICP edit at `stash@{0}` (T075220), wedge at `stash@{2}` (T075049), standards at `stash@{3}` (T074757) — Hermes stashed each as it noticed the new file before its next rebase pass. Reading the `--stat` told me exactly which stash to recover from per file.
- **Polling was right; force-through would have been wrong.** The 5-consecutive-quiet-poll heuristic gave 15s of idle confidence before I committed; Hermes never came back. If I had `rm -f .git/index.lock` and forced through during Hermes' active rebase, I could have corrupted Hermes' #2488 work AND lost mine. Polling cost ~30s wall-clock; the alternative could have cost hours of recovery on both sides.
